Neonatal Komodo dragons emerge from parchment-shelled eggs after a developmental period that is strongly influenced by incubation temperature. When eggs are maintained at a steady 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the interval between oviposition and shell pipping is approximately 49 days [ab = approximately 49 days]. Hatchlings at emergence exhibit a wet weight of around 90 grams [Wwb = around 90 grams] and display a total length at birth of roughly 40 centimeters [Lb = roughly 40 centimeters]. This relatively modest initial body size belies the dramatic ontogenetic changes that will follow as these young reptiles transition from their lecithotrophic, yolk-dependent stage to active hunting. Yolk nutrients sustain neonates during their first few weeks, after which the onset of exogenous feeding marks a critical trophic switch. Juveniles begin actively pursuing small invertebrates and lizards, initiating a phase of rapid somatic growth that will continue for years. The timing of egg deposition and the thermal regime of the nest therefore exert profound effects on offspring quality, with cooler incubation temperatures generally prolonging development and producing slightly larger hatchlings at the cost of extended embryonic exposure to predation and desiccation.

As Komodo dragons progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, their growth rates remain impressive but begin to decelerate as they approach the size thresholds associated with reproductive maturation. In both sexes, the attainment of a total length at puberty of 200 centimeters [Lp = 200 centimeters] is considered a key milestone. At this point, individuals typically weigh approximately 18,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 18,000 grams] in wet weight, reflecting the considerable biomass accumulated over several years of foraging on medium-sized prey such as deer and wild boar. The onset of gonadal activity, however, is not synchronous between sexes; females mature reproductively earlier than males. Under a mean annual thermal regime of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C], which is characteristic of the cooler upland regions of Flores and Komodo Island, first reproduction in females occurs at about 4 years and 5 months of age [tR = at about 4 years and 5 months of age]. Males, by contrast, require a longer developmental interval and typically do not engage in their first successful copulation until approximately 8 years [tR = approximately 8 years] of age, a delay that may be linked to the competitive advantages conferred by larger body size in male-male agonistic encounters during the breeding season. at a temperature of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C]

Adult body size in the Komodo dragon is markedly dimorphic, with females reaching a smaller ultimate size than males. The ultimate wet weight for female individuals is approximately 87,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 87,000 grams], while males routinely attain an ultimate wet weight of 70,000 grams [Wwi = 70,000 grams], though this latter figure can be exceeded in exceptionally large specimens from well-provisioned populations. Correspondingly, the ultimate total length recorded for the species is 240 centimeters [Li = 240 centimeters], representing a six-fold increase from neonatal length. This substantial size disparity between the sexes is thought to reflect divergent selective pressures: larger size in males enhances success in intrasexual combat for access to receptive females, whereas female size may be constrained by the energetic demands of egg production. Gravid females, which are reproductively active adults, excavate deep nesting cavities in sandy soils where they deposit between 15 and 30 leathery-shelled eggs. The energetic investment per clutch is considerable, and females typically do not breed every year, instead exhibiting intermittent reproductive cycles contingent on the recovery of their body condition.

The maximum reproductive rate of the Komodo dragon, expressed in terms of annual fecundity, provides insight into the species potential for population growth under favorable conditions. Field observations indicate that, when maintained at an average ambient temperature of 30.7 °C [T = 30.7 °C], a reproductively active female can produce approximately 22 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 22 eggs per year]. This figure represents the upper bound of reproductive output, as it is derived from optimal thermal regimes that accelerate vitellogenesis and shorten the interval between successive nesting events. In cooler or resource-limited years, however, clutch size and frequency decline substantially, illustrating the sensitivity of reptilian reproductive physiology to environmental variation. The parchment-shelled eggs of this species rely on microbial heat generated within the mound nest to maintain developmental temperatures; thus, the 30.7 °C measurement reflects not the core body temperature of the female but rather the thermal conditions within the incubation chamber during peak egg production. Under these conditions, a female may nest only once annually, but the combination of large clutch size and moderate egg survivorship can still sustain stable population densities across the fragmented island habitats where this apex predator resides.

Longevity in the Komodo dragon is considerable, with maximum lifespan estimates derived from longitudinal mark-recapture studies on the islands of Komodo and Rinca. Under the relatively cool average annual temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] that characterizes these subtropical savanna habitats, the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 62 years [am = approximately 62 years] of age. This extended lifespan is typical of very large reptilian carnivores and is facilitated by low adult mortality rates, a slow pace of life, and the absence of natural predators once individuals exceed a threshold body size. Senescence in this species manifests as a gradual decline in locomotor performance and hunting efficiency, often accompanied by tooth wear and reduced bite force, rather than a sudden reproductive cessation. Older adults may still breed, but their competitive ability within the male hierarchy diminishes. The prolonged period of somatic growth means that individuals may not attain asymptotic body mass until several decades into life, and the physiological death of the organism typically follows a period of progressive deterioration linked to the exhaustion of fat reserves and the eventual failure of vital physiological functions during prolonged dry seasons.
